name: 3-ingredient aquafaba chocolate mousse

source.author: Credited by the poster to river.wellnessdaily (Instagram, English, pasted text)
source.notes: Chickpea-tin brine (aquafaba) whipped to stiff peaks like egg whites, then folded with unsweetened cocoa powder and a splash of sugar-free maple syrup, chilled. The post described it very positively and gave its own macro estimate (claimed: 15 kcal / 1.5 g protein / 3 g carb / 0.1 g fat / 1 g fiber per serving). INDEPENDENT ESTIMATE BELOW DIFFERS SLIGHTLY: aquafaba's nutrition varies noticeably by brand/batch (it's leftover canning liquid, not a standardized ingredient), and 'sugar-free maple syrup' spans a wide range of actual carb content depending on brand (some use sugar alcohols that still show up on a carb count even at low net-impact). This entry's numbers are a from-ingredients estimate, landing in the same ballpark as the poster's claim but a bit higher on carbs — both are genuinely low-calorie either way. Confidence is low given how variable aquafaba and 'sugar-free' syrups are brand-to-brand.

ingredients.note: brand-dependent — some use sugar alcohols; adjust to taste

steps: Drain the aquafaba from a can of chickpeas into a clean mixing bowl.
Whisk with an electric mixer until it forms stiff, fluffy peaks, similar to whipped egg whites.
Gently fold in the cocoa powder and the sugar-free maple syrup, keeping as much of the airy volume as possible.
Divide into 2 servings and chill before serving.

batch_totals.note: Whole batch (2 servings). Genuinely near-zero calorie and fat either way you estimate it — a real novelty: a chocolate-mousse texture with almost no nutritional footprint. Not a protein or fiber source, just a very low-cost sweet treat. Sodium comes from the aquafaba itself (canned-bean brine carries some salt).

him.verdict: Interesting as a near-zero-calorie way to satisfy a chocolate craving on a cut — at ~20 kcal/serving it costs you essentially nothing against a daily deficit. But it brings no protein, no real fiber, and no micronutrients worth noting; this is purely a psychological/craving tool, not a nutritional contributor. A genuinely clever trick to have in the back pocket for evenings when you want something sweet without touching your macros.
flags: ~20 kcal/serving — essentially free against a daily deficit
almost no protein, fat or fiber — not a nutritional contributor, just a low-cost sweet
sodium from the aquafaba itself (~148 mg/serving) — minor but present
result is brand-dependent (aquafaba and sugar-free syrup both vary)
genuinely novel technique if it works as described
suggested_mods: Useful specifically as a craving-management tool on a deficit, not a food to build meals around
If you want some protein in it, folding in a small scoop of chocolate protein powder with the cocoa would turn this into something more substantial (will change the texture/macros though)
Worth trying once to confirm it whips up as described before relying on it regularly

her_preconception.verdict: No safety concerns (chickpea brine, cocoa, no raw egg despite the egg-white-like texture), but it offers essentially nothing toward her prenatal priorities — no folate, iron, choline or calcium in any meaningful amount. It's a fine occasional low-calorie sweet, not a dish that does anything for her nutritionally.
suggested_mods: Fine occasionally as a treat; doesn't need to be a regular part of her intake

cooking_guide: Use the brine from a can of chickpeas, not the chickpeas themselves — it needs to be genuinely liquid, not clumpy, to whip properly.
A completely clean, grease-free bowl matters here just like with egg whites — any residual fat will stop the aquafaba from whipping to stiff peaks.
Whip on a high speed with an electric mixer, not by hand — this takes real volume and time to build, similar to a meringue.
Fold the cocoa and sweetener in GENTLY with a spatula, not with the mixer — stirring vigorously at this stage will deflate the whipped volume you just built.
Chill before serving — this firms up the texture and makes it taste and feel more like a real mousse.
Tip: aquafaba quality varies by brand of canned chickpeas, so if it doesn't whip well the first time, try a different brand next time rather than assuming the technique failed.
